analysis.one_liner: Reallocates California's federal water supply toward farm and city contractors while easing endangered-species protections.
analysis.headline: The House passed the water bill 230-190 in July 2017, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite how California's two big water projects — the federally run Central Valley Project and the State Water Project — are operated. It directs that they be run under a 1994 water-quality agreement 'without regard to' the Endangered Species Act, counts hatchery-born salmon the same as wild fish, lets a state environmental filing substitute for the federal environmental review, and directs Interior to shut down the San Joaquin River salmon restoration settlement. It also bundles items with broader appeal: feasibility studies for new reservoirs, faster federal permitting for water projects, and protections for water-rights holders when federal agencies renew land-use permits.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural water contractors in California's Central Valley — irrigation districts holding large, long-term federal water contracts — gain the most: guaranteed allocation floors, automatic 40-year contract renewals on request, looser water-transfer rules, and far more water delivered in dry years because environmental flow requirements are suspended. Municipal and industrial water agencies also gain promised supply reliability. Dam-building and water storage interests gain feasibility studies and authority to partner with local agencies on construction.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Central Valley Project and State Water Project to be operated under the 1994 Bay-Delta standards 'without regard to' the Endangered Species Act or any other law governing their operations [S4 Sec 108].
Directs the Interior Secretary, on a contractor's request, to renew any long-term Central Valley Project water contract for 40 years [S4 Sec 103].

Guarantees Sacramento Valley agricultural contractors allocations of up to 100% of their contract quantities in wet, above-normal, and favorable below-normal years, and no less than twice the south-of-Delta allocation in other years [S4 Sec 304].

Directs Interior to cease implementing the San Joaquin River Restoration Settlement, the court-approved deal to restore salmon flows to the river, and lets Interior release restoration flows only if all improvements are finished and no landowner or water agency is involuntarily harmed [S4 Sec 113].

Bars Interior and USDA from conditioning or withholding land-use permits on federal land over water rights, and requires federal water rules to be no stricter than California state water law [S4 Sec 703].

Speeds water project permitting by making the Bureau of Reclamation the lead coordinator of all federal reviews and lets project studies be completed within three years at a $3 million federal cost cap [S4 Sec 503, Sec 603].
Orders completion of feasibility studies for new California water storage projects by late 2018 and 2019 and authorizes storage construction if financed with non-federal funds [S4 Sec 201, Sec 203].

analysis.who_pays: Reduced river flows fall on salmon and other fish, on commercial and tribal fishing communities that depend on them, and on communities in the Delta whose water quality depends on fresh water moving through it. The bill also shifts compliance costs away from contractors — no cost of the bill may be imposed on water contractors or California agencies unless voluntary — and it caps what power and water users pay into the fish-restoration fund, leaving restoration shortchanged.
analysis.who_pays_short: Salmon fisheries, tribes, and Delta communities

drawbacks.text: Suspending the Endangered Species Act for Central Valley and State Water Project operations removes the main legal protection for salmon, steelhead, and Delta smelt during the very dry years when they need it most [S4 Sec 108, Sec 111].

Counting hatchery-spawned fish the same as wild-spawned fish in Endangered Species Act decisions could allow species to be listed or protected at levels that mask the collapse of the wild runs [S4 Sec 109].

Ending the San Joaquin River Restoration Settlement unwinds a settlement the federal government, the state, and conservation groups negotiated in court, including a finding in the bill itself that federal funding for it was never fully provided [S4 Sec 113].

In dry years, no mitigation measures would be required for project operations unless quantitative data proves actual harm to species, a standard that favors water deliveries over ecosystems [S4 Sec 111].

No new federal money is authorized for the new storage projects the bill promotes; they may be built only if non-federal financing covers them, so local water users would bear the cost [S4 Sec 107(e)].

The bill bars imposing any cost of the new water rules on contractors or California agencies unless they agree voluntarily, leaving the fiscal burden with the federal taxpayer or unaddressed [S4 Sec 108(c), Sec 303(b)].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The permitting streamlining, storage feasibility studies, and protections for individual water-rights holders have genuine cross-party appeal and appear in other bills both parties support. But the bill's core is a one-directional transfer of water from rivers and fisheries to the contractors holding the largest and cheapest federal water contracts, achieved by suspending the Endangered Species Act and rolling back a court settlement rather than by finding new water. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the reliability gains for contractors come directly at the expense of salmon runs, tribal fisheries, and Delta water quality.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 230-190 along party lines on July 12, 2017, but the Senate committee it was sent to never brought it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative David Valadao introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the new Congress [S1].
It cleared the House 230-190 on July 12, 2017, with 226 of 239 Republicans voting yes and 4 of 194 Democrats voting yes [S8].

Just before final passage, Democrats offered a motion to recommit instructing the bill to ensure adequate water supplies for fighting wildfires; it failed 189-230, with only 2 Republicans supporting it [S7].
The Senate received the bill on July 18, 2017 and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which took no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, Central Valley farm water contractors did not get the Endangered Species Act waiver, guaranteed allocations, or 40-year contract renewals; salmon runs, tribal and commercial fishing communities, and Delta communities kept the existing legal protections. The House passage still served as a template for later California water rider efforts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Salmon fisheries, tribes, and Delta communities

for.name: Rep. David Valadao
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and shepherded it to House passage.

for.name: 226 of 239 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage of the bill.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the structured rule (H. Res. 431) that brought the bill to the floor with one hour of debate and a limited set of amendments.

for.name: National Resources Defense Council
for.role: Conservation group; party to the San Joaquin River settlement the bill would unwind
for.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's rollback of the San Joaquin River restoration settlement and Endangered Species Act protections.

against.name: 183 of 194 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, and 187 of them backed a motion to recommit to add wildfire water-supply language.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 18, 2017 and scheduled no markup or floor action for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 226 of 239 Republicans voted yes while only 4 of 194 Democrats did; on the Democrats' pre-passage motion, just 2 Republicans joined 187 Democrats.

industries.industry: Central Valley agricultural water contractors (irrigation districts and agribusiness)
industries.note: The bill locks in these contractors' federal water deliveries — guaranteed allocation floors, 40-year contract renewals on request, relaxed transfer rules — while suspending the Endangered Species Act for project operations. The additional water comes out of river flows that fisheries and Delta communities depend on.

industries.industry: Commercial, recreational, and tribal salmon fishing
industries.note: Reduced river flows, ESA waivers, hatchery fish counted as wild, and the shutdown of the San Joaquin River restoration settlement all threaten the salmon runs the fishing economy and tribes rely on.
The bill promises reliable supplies to municipal and industrial users and lets them reschedule contract water between years, which helps city water customers during droughts.

industries.industry: Water storage and dam construction interests
industries.note: Feasibility studies are ordered for new reservoirs and construction is authorized with non-federal financing, but no new federal money is provided, so the industry gains opportunity while local water users bear the cost.

Payments into the fish-restoration fund are re-pegged to $4 per megawatt-hour on project power instead of $12 per acre-foot on water, lowering what power users pay for the environmental mitigation they benefit from.
